stories.body:
How the United States abandoned the future.

Simon Curtis is an associate professor in International Relations at the University of Surrey, and a WISC Global Fellow at the Development Research Institute at New York University.

Ian Klaus is the founding director of Carnegie Endowment for International Peace California Center.

They are co-authors of “The Belt and Road City: Geopolitics, Urbanization, and China’s Search for a New International Order” (2024, Yale University Press).

The application of power, especially for Great Powers, is an exercise in time. In an auspicious year — the 250th since its founding — the United States has looked back to its revolutionary past but has shown little indication of developing a clear vision for its future. And with little apparent inclination to do so, rarely has the country seemed more adrift in the flow of history. This comes at a bad time. China’s rise has given the United States a strategic competitor intent on building its own version of tomorrow.

As the Trump administration uses its second term to try to flex the sinews of American might, the sources of American power have never seemed less well understood. The sense of purpose and destiny, and the vision and confidence of previous generations, have been replaced by confusion, division and a loss of moral clarity. Many truths once held to be self-evident are now questioned. Perhaps what has been most keenly lost is the sense that the wellsprings of national strength come from thinking intergenerationally and harnessing the power of the future, both in terms of planning and rhetoric.

But this is the wrong moment to abandon future generations. China has been preparing for decades to rival the United States in shaping the institutions and architecture of international order — first slowly and cautiously, and now increasingly assertively. China has been playing a long geopolitical game; one the United States is currently losing. In fact, it is essentially sitting out the game, trapped in nostalgia and short-termism, as China consciously builds institutions and infrastructures designed to project power across decades.

The real contest between China and the United States is not the surface froth of conflict over tariffs, shifting military capabilities, or even the development of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence or clean energy. It is a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.

The Loss Of The Future

One of the most striking features of the contemporary moment in the United States, and in the West more generally, is the sense of temporal disorientation. Once, dreams of building a better tomorrow powered the United States to victory in the Cold War. For the West, a strand of history did end with the fall of the Berlin Wall, just not in the way we expected. From 1989 onward, rather than the unending triumph of a liberal order, the West faced a strange series of crises through which it lost the historical thread altogether.

The Cold War and its most symbolic moments were an intergenerational game. The United States once reached for the stars with state-guided Cold War technological moonshots, built the architecture of a new liberal international order and defended it with a sense of intergenerational collective mission, and shaped cities and infrastructures around the world with the power of its economic model. Today, the U.S. is unmoored from that sense of historical destiny.

Much of this disorientation can be traced to cultural changes in the fabric of American society. Among them is its cultural orientation to time. This temporal disorientation takes multiple forms — but in each the future becomes opaque.

The Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement that swept Donald Trump to power began as a reaction to the failed promises of globalization, and discontent over the priorities of elites and their failures to address the concerns of everyday Americans. But as its name suggests, its orientation to time is deeply nostalgic; a wistful longing for some poorly articulated and mythical past. Part of MAGA’s failure in government stems from its lack of a compelling future-oriented vision for either domestic or international society.

But the roots of America’s problems in articulating a compelling future go far beyond MAGA. It is part of a broader crisis of time that the West has wrestled with throughout modernity. For many decades now, the political and economic culture seems trapped in a perpetual present that emphasizes short-term cycles: two-year midterm electoral cycles, four-year turnarounds in administrations whose legislative achievements are immediately unpicked by the next regime, quarterly business cycles that curtail long-term investment, 24-hour news cycles, even the rapid-fire video reels that characterize social media consumption today are but the latest manifestation of a long trend.

“The real contest between China and the United States is … a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.”

Prior to the end of the Cold War, the cultural critic Frederic Jameson sought to chart and diagnose our more recent confusion in time: the lost threads of historical narrative, the temporal dislocation and stasis of our politics. When Jameson described the cultural condition of postmodernity, he was describing a collective loss of confidence in the futures that modernity once promised; its productive energies now exhausted, history now but a mosaic and collage constructed selectively by the powerful, collective purpose dissolved in an acid of consumerist images and desires, the idea of building a future utopia no longer something that we can believe in without irony. For decades this state of stasis was undisturbed by a significant external threat or real geopolitical competitor, and so its corrosive effects were overlooked. Both time and the rare moment of unipolar power that emerged in the 1990s were squandered.

Now two such challenges disturb this malaise: the rise of China and the existential threat of climate change. And yet the seemingly permanent constraint on the temporal horizon is effectively neutering the West’s ability to meet either challenge.

Cycles Of Decay & Renewal

We needn’t be so hard on Americans. As the Cameroonian historian Achille Mbembe has noted , the West at large has foreclosed on the idea of any world to come or any imagined future. Exit is impossible, he winks in French; the longue durée is a dead idea. But of course, most Western powers are not great powers, and their roles in geopolitics — even when united in suprajurisdictions like the European Union — don’t rival the world-shaping power of the United States.

But China’s role does. Unlike the United States today, China builds its geopolitical strategies over decades. Its one-party state rolls on in pursuit of an international environment that better reflects its own domestic values and priorities, unperturbed by the political or economic storms of the present, or the vicissitudes of democratic politics. Democracies must find a way to somehow match the ability of China to dictate a geopolitical strategy that unfolds over decades if they are to build new institutions that successfully compete in the long game.

Equally disconcerting has been the eruption, at the margins of our consciousness and culture, of the concept of deep time and the realization that our societies and economies are intrinsically entangled with the systems of the natural world; that the Anthropocene is a reality that any sustainable future must come to terms with, and that untrammeled consumption and growth bring with them their own reckonings.

The deep time of the Anthropocene necessitates stretching our temporal horizon much further into both past and future and thinking about the legacies we leave to future generations around the climate and intergenerational justice. It alerts us to the reality that we must now leave behind nostalgia and expand our temporal imaginations.

China has done so, thinking through these challenges in ways that seek to capture the future. As one pillar of its bid for international leadership, it is developing an “ ecological civilization ” to bridge long-term geopolitical positioning and the challenge of the Anthropocene by constructing the technologies, infrastructures and cities that might make the concept a reality.

These are the kinds of world-shaping energies and ambitions that the United States once had. The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui. This may be the normal trajectory for great powers, whose civilizational energies, once expended, can tail off into decline. Can a new generation of Americans, now quite far removed in time from its founders, recover within themselves and within these foundational principles, the sources of renewal that will allow them to break with the gravitational pull of history’s cycles of decline and fall?

For, if not, then the citizens of the United States, so long in the vanguard of shaping and building the future via their vast productive energies, innovative capacities and institutions, may end up living in somebody else’s future.

Grand Strategy & Scale

The Cold War-era American diplomat George Kennan thought the geography of the United States naturally determined its geopolitics. And while the bicoastal nature of the country has offered advantages and shaped policies, the scope of U.S. influence has scaled well beyond the contours of its geography.

“The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui.”

Since World War II, the United States has scaled its influence in notable ways. First, it has linked domestic institutions and international order. A historic example is how Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal in the 1930s and 1940s was woven into the fabric of the United Nations and other nascent international institutions, as the U.S. shouldered the responsibility of crafting a new international order from the ruins of World War II.

It is in vogue now to disparage the Biden Administration’s foreign policy, but attention to Gaza or the Afghanistan exit should not distract from how well the administration understood this linkage between domestic and transnational scale, and implicitly time. The centerpiece of Biden’s domestic and international program — and the hinge between the two — was the 2021 Inflation Reduction Act, which sought to kickstart a green energy transition that would bring jobs to the country’s post-industrial heartlands. Jake Sullivan, Biden’s former national security adviser, described this aim as turning the Rust Belt into a “cobalt corridor,” while also renewing U.S. leadership abroad by helping to craft solutions to the intractable international challenge of climate change. This initial attempt to build a new connecting bridge between domestic and international renewal stalled and was then decisively reversed in places upon Trump’s return.

One crucial strategic approach among all U.S. administrations since World War II has been nurturing the alliance system, which allowed the United States to achieve its hegemonic position and, until recently, presented a great challenge to China’s ambitions. The Trump Administration’s myopia has made it nearly impossible for the United States to predictably shape events beyond its borders, especially in the long run.

Gone now are two notable long-held U.S. strategic advantages: a linkage between the domestic agenda and foreign policy, which enabled intergenerational strategic investments, and the robust network of allies and institutions that allowed it to project its power and values. To the loss of the future on a temporal scale, we must add the loss on a spatial scale: a failure to think across both time and space.

The resources needed to power success in the 21st century are dispersed around the globe: supply chains of critical minerals and rare earths, sustainable energy resources, pools of talent and expertise. These are the resources required to sustain leadership in the emerging geopolitics of artificial intelligence, the transition to sustainable clean energy and biotechnology.

It has never been enough to be the most innovative, to dominate the frontiers of technological innovation. Jeffrey Ding, a George Washington University scholar whose work has become increasingly influential in debates about U.S.-China competition, argues that technological contests between great powers are ultimately won not by breakthrough inventions but by the patient and long-term work of diffusion. This tracks with the wider histories of technology by scholars like Carolyn Marvin and David Edgerton that focus on uptake or adoption rather than invention.

The societies that prevail are those that can construct infrastructures, train people, build institutions and reorganize production around new technologies. This is the painstaking work of decades, rather than the one-time boost that comes from inventing a new frontier technology. This historical lesson is especially relevant to the geopolitical competition between the United States and China today, where the U.S. holds a lead at the frontier but has thought less about diffusion.

Access to transnational resources requires not just maintaining good international relationships but also constructing and controlling intricate transnational infrastructure . This is exactly what China’s Belt and Road Initiative has been building over the last 13 years. Its new Silk Roads are the filaments of rail, road, maritime commerce, digital systems, energy transmission and smart cities that can generate, shape and carry flows of resources, goods, people and influence. By building infrastructure and shaping cities far beyond its borders, China is working to ensure that momentum is angled toward its own growing center of gravity.

China is putting production, scale and control over key transnational resources at the heart of its foreign policy. It is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning. This model diverges significantly from Washington’s. This is China’s long game.

In the mid-2010s, before becoming one of Washington’s most influential China strategists, Rush Doshi was a doctoral researcher at Harvard University embarking on an unusually painstaking exercise. He sifted through three decades of Chinese-language speeches, policy documents, party communiqués and military writings in search of an answer to a simple question: Did China really have a coherent strategy for challenging American primacy? Rather than a sudden turn under Chinese President Xi Jinping, Doshi found evidence of a remarkably consistent long-term effort to blunt, and eventually displace, U.S. dominance in the post-World War II international order.

“China is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning.”

Under Xi’s leadership over the last decade and more, this long-term strategy has accelerated. The Belt and Road Initiative is its material infrastructural core, winding its way from ports in the Indian Ocean and rail corridors across Central Asia into Europe to fiber-optic cables reaching down through Pakistan to East Africa, and to ambitions for transcontinental power transmission systems and digital infrastructures.

By building out these material footings, China is constructing infrastructures to carry the leading technological transformations that will shape this century, and perhaps beyond. Artificial intelligence and an alternative internet are enrolling states into China’s enlarging sociotechnical system across Eurasia and Africa. The types of domestic transformations, including the most intense period of urbanization in human history and a radical reinvention of the domestic economy, have changed the nature of Chinese cities and infrastructure, generating cutting-edge modern metropolises such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chongqing, and are now being transmitted to other countries with Chinese labor, expertise and capital.

And because cities reflect the dominant societies that create them, Chinese influence will spread outward, just as new forms of connectivity will place China at the core of a new material and economic order. In its recently unveiled 15th Five-Year Plan , Beijing doubled down on the industrial strategy of using state economic planning to drive investment in technology, infrastructure and dominance of critical supply chains that has underpinned its rise for four decades. Read Noema in print.

It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory. The United States continues to be a world leader in many frontier technologies, including artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, cloud computing infrastructure, biotechnology platforms, space launch systems and quantum computing research. But the old free market model of cascading benefits from private enterprise and investment that then flow throughout the economy is now being pitted against a very different model: a huge state willing to carefully direct its vast resources to diffuse technology throughout its own society and, via the mechanisms of transnational infrastructure it is building beyond its own borders, to reshape international society.

Although the commanding heights of creativity and innovation may continue to reside in the U.S., China is building the infrastructures of diffusion that may ultimately extract the greatest benefit from those innovations, increasing its soft power, influence and appeal to other states along the way.

The big labs of Silicon Valley are currently gripped by fear that China’s approach to opening its AI models to international partners may undermine the closed-source, proprietary model approach developed by U.S. firms and give China growing global influence in the AI systems race. As Washington well knows, China has already developed significant control over many of the world’s critical supply chains needed for those technologies, including those for processed rare earths vital for building the digital architectures and artificial intelligences of the future, and for batteries and robotics.

As Sullivan has argued, it will be the societies that most successfully capture and deploy resources at scale that win the future, and many of those resources reside far from America’s shores. These are the “nodes of leverage,” as Sullivan describes them. Donald Trump found this out when trying to apply pressure through tariffs on China.

There are challenges to be sure. China has an aging population, a burgeoning debt cloud, an extended property sector crisis and still lacks genuine soft power and allies. Its increasingly centralized political system could yet become a source of weakness. And yet it has realized that successful grand strategy today requires thinking about space and time in ways that register the importance of both transnational scale and the long term. If the U.S. is to compete successfully, it will need to remember how to think in those terms.

In Search Of Time Future

How can the United States rework its political culture and institutions to take these concerns on board and shape its strategic orientation toward a new form of international society fit for the current century?

Although we have come to think that the unfettered free market and capitalism’s unimpeded creative energy led to the Soviet Union’s defeat, this reflects historical forgetfulness. During the Cold War, the federal government invested both at home and abroad to shape the outcome of that hegemonic contest.

“It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory.”

Many constituents in the U.S. have forgotten the historical importance of what the Harvard historian Charles Maier called the “ Project-State ” – states driven by a deep sense of ideological and historical mission that use their resources to generate far-reaching social, political and economic transformation. Such states might be democratic or authoritarian in character and ideological mission. Maier writes of the history of Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia, but also of the United States under President Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal, and the restructuring of both domestic and international society that Roosevelt’s project-state enacted.

The project-state, by its very nature, plays a long game. It cannot exist in the culture of short-termism and the diminished temporal horizon of contemporary America. Today, China, with its clear sense of ideological mission and long-term strategic planning, more closely resembles the history-making project-states of the past. Maier, now in his late 80s, has expressed concern that the U.S. — hollowed out by market ideology, rising populism and a loss of national cohesion and democratic mission — has forgotten its sense of itself as a collective, intergenerational history-shaping project.

Success for great powers needs long-term purpose: a shaping vision of how to build a better domestic and international society that can solve the pressing problems of the day without discounting the future. If it is to change direction, future American power would need to consider and build into its strategic planning all of the issues raised here: the relationship between state industrial policy and technological innovation, the way in which innovations are diffused through society, as well as the infrastructures and urban environments needed to shape lives through technological advance — not just domestically but transnationally.

Above all, democracies must transcend their culture of short-termism and treat rebuilding their domestic and shared international societies as a long-term intergenerational project. Rather than simply looking back on its 250th anniversary, the United States must play the long game and consider the next 250 years.

Sullivan’s instinct that the material well-being and economic prospects of the middle and working classes must be the starting point is a good one, as is the deliberate linking of international and domestic society. But more needs to be done to fully conceptualize and forge a new link between them.

Many paths might be taken, but some more interesting and influential debates are underway that could shape a post-Trump and post-MAGA direction. The so-called abundance agenda, for all the attention and subsequent criticism it received, provides a helpful template for moving beyond the now-exhausted laissez-faire of the last half-century.

Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argue for accelerating the latent yet blocked productive potential of American technology and society. They seek to rediscover the lost optimism and long-termism that once defined America — a new socio-technical imaginary of the future — alongside the institutional and state capability needed to realize it.

America’s ability to construct a future better than its past, despite many of the technological building blocks already in place, is, they argue, strangled by red tape, an excessively legalistic culture, increasingly polarized politics, and most crucially, a loss of the state’s capacity to build, coordinate and direct long-term national development.

In many domains like clean energy, scientific and biomedical innovation, technological breakthroughs exist, but the infrastructures of diffusion are absent because of a lack of state-driven investment and fragmented governance. Transmission and grid infrastructure for solar, wind, geothermal and nuclear technologies are lagging. America is a leader in biomedical science, but greater state investment in scientific institutions could drive research into real-world applications and rollouts. America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.

The abundance agenda is animated by the transformative potential of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence, clean energy, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, but it requires technological innovation to be matched by the institutional ability to deploy it through renewed investment in infrastructure, scientific research, energy transmission and the transition to a sustainable energy system.

At its heart is a politics of building: restoring the state’s capacity not merely to regulate markets, but also to shape them in pursuit of long-term national renewal. One missing policy mechanism is a sovereign infrastructure institution, such as a Strategic Investment Fund , that could unlock private capital reluctant to take on the long-term investment risks required for major national and international infrastructure projects. In this way, vast pools of private capital may be unlocked that could help the United States and its allies match the infrastructure-building scale and strategic reach of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

“America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.”

When the United States constructed the post-World War II architecture, it inevitably brought many elements of its own domestic experience to that task. The ideological underpinnings of Roosevelt’s New Deal, with its focus on federal state-led programs of reform and renewal after the Great Depression, also shaped many of the financial and institutional governance structures of the new multilateral order — specifically the United Nations. This established a link between a great power state’s domestic agenda and its ability to craft a wider international order. The New Deal emerged out of the New York context, where Roosevelt cut his teeth politically before becoming president.

Today, however, technology is likely to be at the core of any renewal of the United States’ social contract, so we must look to California for clues about its development. The transformational impact on society of advances in artificial intelligence will test what type of political economy will shape America and its key allies’ futures.

California’s outgoing governor, Gavin Newsom, who’s also potentially gearing up for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, has had a ringside seat as Silicon Valley has pushed the boundaries of AI in recent years. Newsom has watched this development and tried to think about the way progressives can harness it to improve society. Rather than accepting the current paradigm, his progressive backers have been drawn to the idea of an “ AI New Deal ,” echoing an earlier time of similar economic instability and rising authoritarian powers. He has also referenced the abundance agenda in state legislation and argued for an “abundant mindset.”

Newsom has expressed concern for the disruptive and potentially harmful effects of AI for American workers, issuing executive orders directing state agencies, academia and industry to think about safety nets for displaced workers, including state subsidies incentivizing companies to retain and upskill employees, as well as exploring the idea of “ universal basic capital ” providing workers with a stake in asset funds to offset wage losses brought about by AI. Newsom seems aware of the need for a social compact to absorb short-term shocks from the technology.

If Newsom were to gain the Democratic nomination in 2028, then his dispositions may well be an indication of America’s future direction — a subnational model transposed to the larger scale canvas of national and international politics, as well as a new direction in that perennial question of how to link the domestic to the international scale, and thus to the shaping of international order.

Although many pathways may be taken in the post-Trump, post-MAGA world, the ideas being pursued by thinkers, policymakers and politicians such as Newsom, Sullivan, and Klein and Thompson all point to the need to link American domestic renewal with international order. Sullivan’s foreign policy for the middle classes sought to learn from Trump’s appeal to working-class Americans.

But where Trump’s instinctively treats America’s relationship with the rest of the world and its allies as a zero-sum game, Sullivan recognizes that the relationship must be bidirectional and therefore — mutually beneficial. U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership. Trump’s approach breaks the symbiotic connection between a beneficial international order and the public goods and advantages that flow from it. Critically, it also threatens to deny the United States the transnational scale and reach to compete effectively with China if its allies turn away.

Here then is a coda, from, of all places, Angola. In December 2024, Biden became the first American president in nearly a decade to visit a sub-Saharan African country. For it was in Angola that one of the flagship transnational infrastructure projects of the U.S.-led G7 Partnership for Global Infrastructure Investment (PGII) was to begin — the Lobito Trans-Africa Corridor project — a strategic transport and logistics corridor to connect the port city of Lobito by railway to the interior of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, areas rich in critical minerals like cobalt, copper and other rare earths for the technological transitions in both clean energy and AI. Angola symbolized a shift in American foreign policy toward long-term investment in transnational infrastructure, driven by a dawning realization of China’s growing influence.

“U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership.”

With the Trans-Africa Corridor project and the even more ambitious India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor project under the Biden administration, the U.S. and its allies had started to copy some of China’s playbook: a focus on maritime ports, transport connectivity through corridor development, securing supply chains of critical minerals, and support for digital infrastructure. The big difference was the central role of private-sector finance, rather than direct state investment as in the Chinese model.

Transnational infrastructure as geopolitics had belatedly made its way to the core of U.S. foreign policy; an overdue turn to thinking about the nature of strategic competition on both spatial and temporal scales. With the change in administration, America moved away from this approach.

The Twilight Of Primacy?

Paths to renewal and decline are both on offer. If the wrong path is taken, then the moment of American primacy will have lasted about a century — a familiar historical pattern.

A more exceptional path would be for a Great Power to reforge that link between a compelling renewed domestic social, political and economic model, and a different form of international order that crafts a new future for the United States and others. At the same time, China is also feeling its way toward its own version of such a link. And, as Xi has made clear time and again, China feels that time is on its side.

Great powers are ultimately judged not by the wealth they accumulate or the weapons they possess, but by the futures they can persuade others to inhabit. All of the major challenges that face humanity — the development of artificial intelligence, the transition to clean and sustainable energy, the working out of a new model for the world economy, the relationship of people to their political institutions, the balance of power between ambitious and competitive states — are subsumed by this overarching task of linking a successful domestic paradigm to the architecture of international order.

Can the next generation of U.S. leadership rise to these challenges as their forebears once did? The central question facing this generation of policymakers is whose future they want Americans to live in: the one they build, or somebody else’s.

stories.title: The Geopolitical Earthquake of the Iran War
stories.summary: The Middle East has been turned into a giant theater of war. And it may not stop there. The post The Geopolitical Earthquake of the Iran War appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

The Iran War has claimed thousands of lives, most of them in Iran itself. The war has cost Iran as much as $300 billion in economic damage. For its part, the Pentagon spent nearly $44 billion through mid-September to wreak that amount of havoc. For advocates of the war—but no one else—that’s a good return on investment.

Because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions in shipments of oil and gas, people all over the world have experienced the war through increased prices for energy, transportation, and food. The ripple effects through the global economy of record high prices for diesel have been devastating for farmers , truckers, and the mining sector. Back in August, the International Monetary Fund warned that the war, if it continues, could trigger a global economic recession.

And the war is continuing—even though Iran and its adversaries have at least temporarily stepped back from direct attacks and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has recovered to a certain extent (Iranian shipments excluded). At the UN General Assembly last month, Donald Trump promised (yet again) that he would annihilate Iran if the country doesn’t agree to some kind of peace deal. Despite the fact that the Iranian economy is reeling as a result of war and sanctions, which the government in Tehran is now acknowledging , Iranian leaders have pledged not to surrender.

As if these effects aren’t enough, the Iran War is also setting into motion a number of other geopolitical transformations—in Yemen, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, the Gulf states, and even further afield. Trump and his Israeli partner-in-crime Benjamin Netanyahu expected a quick war, a tidy regime change in Tehran, and the collapse of its “axis of resistance.”

Instead they now face a Pandora’s boxful of unintended consequences.

Yemen’s Forever War

Not far from the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, lies Bab al-Mandab. This chokepoint, which controls traffic in and out of the Red Sea and the Suez Canal at its northernmost point, is responsible for 10 percent of global trade . During the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia redirected the flow of its oil westward through a pipeline to its Red Sea ports, thus increasing the importance of Bab al-Mandab.

But now the Saudis face attacks from the Houthis, a group of Yemenis allied with Iran that have been operating out of an enclave in the north of the country along the Red Sea and not far from the strait. Beginning last decade, the Saudis backed the government of Yemen in its attempts to defeat the Houthis and unify the country, an effort that ultimately failed and forced a ceasefire back in 2022.

Thanks largely to the war in Iran, however, that ceasefire is over. The Houthis have decided to take this opportunity to break out of their enclave to seize territory along the Red Sea— grabbing the port of Mokha in mid-September—and interrupt shipping through Bab al-Mandab. They have also used rather sophisticated weaponry to attack energy infrastructure—including the aforementioned East-West pipeline—throughout Saudi Arabia.

In response, the Saudi-backed Yemeni government has declared all-out war against the Houthis. Where the Saudis go, the Trump administration is sure to follow. Reports The New York Times :

More than 200 U.S. intelligence and military analysts are assisting the Saudi government in command centers inside the kingdom, helping to analyze and select targets in support of its Yemeni allies, according to one current and one former U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. The United States is also providing aerial refueling for Saudi warplanes conducting defensive air patrols, they added.

Saudi assistance enabled Yemeni government forces to retake the port of Mokha this week.

In its attacks on the Houthis last year, the Trump administration committed war crimes – killing dozens of African migrants in a strike on a detention center , killing 80 civilians in a bombing of port infrastructure , and assisting Saudi attacks on schools, hospitals, and markets. It shrugged off those charges, much as earlier administrations failed to reckon with their involvement in the initial Saudi bombings that turned Yemen into a hellscape and led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of civilians .

Now, however, the Trump administration faces an additional risk. Its efforts against Iran are increasingly linked to the Saudi campaign to eradicate the Houthis, making another “forever war” in the region all the more likely.

The Iraqi Vacuum

As negotiated by the Biden administration, the last U.S. troops finally left Iraq last week, 23 years after the U.S. war there began and 12 years after U.S. soldiers returned to the country to battle the Islamic State. The Americans leave behind a deeply corrupt state riven by ethnic and political divisions. The U.S. invasion in 2003 and the inept state-building that followed the fall of Saddam Hussein also created an opportunity for Iran to increase its influence in the country through Shi’ite clerics and paramilitary forces.

September 30 was supposed to be the deadline not only for U.S. troop withdrawal but also the disarmament of Iranian-backed militias. The first happened; the second has been postponed until June 30. The militias are likely to ignore this second deadline as well.

The Iranian-aligned Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) have been incorporated into the Iraqi military, but some forces close to Iran remain on the outside. Even the PMF is not necessarily subordinate to the state. “State status gives a faction money, offices, access, and political protection,” writes Ameer Al-Auqaili at FPIF . “A separate command structure leaves room for independent operations.”

Those independent operations, conducted by a coalition of forces known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, have apparently included an attack last month, coordinated with the Houthis, on the Saudi East-West pipeline. Back in July, the U.S. military joined the Saudis in attacks on the PMF. Iraq has thus become another front in the Iran War: seven of the 18 U.S. combat deaths in that war have occurred in Iraq. Although Trump called the Iraq War a “very expensive excursion into hell,” he has already gone down that road with Iran, and more attacks on the PMF as part of that war may be in the offing.

Even as approximately 1,500 U.S. personnel leave Iraq, the Trump administration is sending another aircraft carrier to the region, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, with 10,000 sailors and Marines. According to Baghdad-based political analyst Ahmed Younis , the U.S. force withdrawal from Iraq raises “the possibility that Iran’s proxies will feel increasingly empowered in the absence of a Western military presence. These groups may attempt to expand their role in shaping state policies and consolidating their presence within key institutions.” That, plus a revival of the Islamic State, might prompt Trump to send U.S. troops back into Iraq.

Welcome to a second road to hell, this one paved with all manner of Trump’s intentions.

Axis of Resistance Over?

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has focused not only on destroying Hamas in Gaza. He has set his sights on eradicating Iran’s entire “axis of resistance.” Toward that end, Israel has attempted to eliminate Hezbollah in Lebanon and reduce Iranian influence in Syria.

To be sure, Netanyahu wants to “solve” the Palestinian problem by displacing and disenfranchising the population. But Iran is by far the more powerful actor in the region, and Netanyahu dearly wants to uproot what he considers the core threat facing Israel.

Israel managed to kneecap the Hezbollah leadership in Lebanon through a campaign of booby-trapped pagers and walkie-talkies alongside a 66-day campaign of airstrikes and ground operations. Israeli forces occupied southern Lebanon, destroying entire towns and establishing five military bases, and set about killing the replacements to the replacements of the Hezbollah leadership. At the same time, taking the degradation of Hezbollah as a signal, Syrian rebels pushed out the Iran-aligned regime of Bashar al-Assad in Syria.

But Iran hasn’t lost its influence in the two countries. Hezbollah managed to rebuild, with the help of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards , in time to launch missiles at Israel after the Iran War began. Israel estimates that Hezbollah, now reorganized around smaller cells, has as many as 15,000 rockets and missiles and is now investing into more drones. The myth that Israel can completely eradicate its adversaries applies as much to Hezbollah as it does to Hamas, which continues to operate in Gaza despite months of punishing air strikes and incursions by Israeli Defense Forces.

Iranian influence in Syria certainly took a nosedive when Assad was pushed from power. Relations between Tehran and the new government of Ahmed al-Sharaa remain frozen . But at the community level, Iranian influence persists, either in the form of religious identification (for the Shia population), political sympathies (in favor of Tehran in its war against the United States and Israel), and even military (such as the Syrian Islamic Resistance Front and various Alawite paramilitaries).

Further afield, Iran has conducted limited operations in Europe. Tehran launched a drone attack against a British military base in Cyprus back in March. Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, a pro-Iranian outfit, has claimed responsibility for a string of attacks on financial institutions and Jewish sites across Europe. Most recently, the United States withdrew 12 bombers from a British airbase in anticipation of an expected Iranian drone attack, although it’s impossible at this point to confirm Iran’s involvement in the plot.

The point here is not to exaggerate an Iranian threat to justify continued military operations against the country, continued U.S. military presence in the region, or continued Israeli efforts to eliminate what it considers an “existential threat.” Quite the contrary: Iranian influence remains as durable in the region as the regime appears to be in Tehran. No amount of military force short of nuclear apocalypse is likely to change that. Israel has tried, and it has failed, both alone and with the United States. The axis of resistance is not exactly stronger after these many attempts to kill it, but it hasn’t disappeared either.

As any practitioner of jujitsu can tell you, resistance grows fiercer the more you push directly against it. A ceasefire, a peace deal with Iran, a meaningful political engagement with Iranian allies in the region: in the long run, such sideways strategies that rely on balance and leverage will prove far more effect in dissolving an axis of resistance.

stories.body:
Identity and the alias nation.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Even if we know it is the way of history, it is nonetheless jarring to witness time and again the return of the repressed in the cultural and political life of nations. It is never over, even after the fat lady sings.

The fat lady sang twice in Germany, first after Nazism was roundly defeated in World War II and second, after the Berlin Wall fell, the Soviet bloc collapsed and “history ended.” Only decades later are we seeing an eruption of all that was left unsettled with the steady rise of neo-Nazi parties, mainly in former East Germany, and the demise of the mainstream political coalitions that were the pillars of post-war liberal democracy.

Looking Back To Three Decades Ago

Some three decades ago, New Perspectives Quarterly (NPQ) published an issue focused on the reignited embers of nationalism in Germany. It reads like a chronicle of the future foretelling the tremors shaking Europe’s most powerful country today.

Contributors to that issue ranged from Daniel Cohn-Bendit, the celebrated May ‘68 rabble-rouser and then-Green Party’s deputy mayor of Frankfurt, to the controversial playwright Hans Jürgen Syberberg, who broke post-war taboos with his movie, “Hitler: A Film From Germany.” Other contributors included Germany’s president at the time, Richard von Weizsäcker and then-foreign minister Hans Dietrich Genscher, whose essay was titled “Nationalism Has No Home in Germany.”

Even then, the issues that stirred the most virulent passions were around the influx of immigrants, lenient asylum policies and the “yearning for a lost sense of belonging.” At the time, isolated gangs were firebombing immigrant homes. Today, those sentiments have been channeled into political parties that garner as high as 44% of the vote in regional elections.

The introduction I wrote to that long-ago NPQ edition read: “Now that the long post-war parole is over, will Germany prove to be reformed or a repeat offender? Unable to face itself, Germany for decades assumed an identity for the benefit of others in order to absolve its crimes. It has become an alias nation hiding its soiled soul under the bushel of NATO and the European community, which, above all else, institutionalizes the liberal ideal of a rational order over a national one.”

Citing the filmmaker Syberberg on why the “democratic repression” associated with rational liberalism cannot forever bury the soul, it continued: “If the cool head allows the passions of the soil no expression, then those underground passions will surface in the ugliest form time and again. A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed instead of evolve a new identity based on the open experience of a new reality.”

Syberberg argued that “after the war, intellectuals stood on the tradition of the Enlightenment and a hegemonic rationalism that focused on the head at the expense of the heart. Culture is built upon the way the light falls on the trees, the way the heavens look at night from the familiarity of a particular place where people live and feel a sense of belonging to a unique way of life, to our garden plots, folk tales and Teutonic fantasies.

“Yet we have felt compelled in Germany to repress this uniqueness. We feel safe excelling at mathematics, physics, business. Our people, dominated by facts and figures, are satisfied to dance around the golden calf of materialism and the strong Deutschmark. We are very efficient and methodical. But where is the heart?”

“Heimat,” or homeland, he went on, “was one of the aesthetic subjects that was forbidden territory after the war.” When the Cold War ended and the wall came down, 15 million people became orphans from an East Germany that no longer existed. “They have a strong sense of Heimat precisely because they have lost their homeland,” Syberberg said. “People need food and shelter, but they also need love, community, a home. This is part of the natural function of being human.”

“A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed instead of evolve a new identity based on the open experience of a new reality.”

To the filmmaker, the extremism of gangs bombing the homes of immigrants was “frightening, like wild animals.” But he thought it was not enough to condemn it; he also needed to understand “what it is in the air nourishing it.” For him, it was a “reaction not fully formed” springing from the wound of historical dislocation and the prohibition, both explicit and implicit, against cherishing one’s own identity when strangers were welcomed.

Heiner Müller, the liberal playwright and counterpoint to Syberberg on the German literary scene, offered much the same analysis. He too addressed the dislocation of East Germans after the end of the Cold War. Today, the strongholds of the neo-Nazi parties are in the former East.

“After the death of socialism as epitomized by the GDR, Germany’s new demon has become neo-Nazi extremism,” he said. “This should surprise no one. With the demise of socialism, and then reunification, a vacuum was created. Capitalism no longer had an enemy, which meant it no longer had an alibi when people failed to thrive. In the wake of discredited left-wing ideologies, right-wing extremism has simply assumed the role of capitalism’s harshest critic.”

For Müller, “there can be no dialogue with the neo-Nazis. They are not interested in dialogue. They are merely following their own logic: the logic of the void. And they are filling the void with nationalism. In the 19th century, radicals sought to appease the ‘God is dead’ trauma through socialism. Today, not only is God dead, but utopias have vanished. There are no values left. From this extends freedom — but also longing — to belong, to be part of a group, a community, a nation.

“The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West,” Müller presciently remarked.

When I spoke in those days to Cohn-Bendit, aka “Danny the Red” of the May ‘68 Paris student uprising, he focused as well on former East Germany, where most of the bombings took place. As he put it, “People in the East unrealistically thought unification would bring their living standards up to the level of the West overnight. But that will take decades. In reality, their life will get worse before it gets better, and so they face a future of fear and uncertainty.

“What happens when you throw 400,000 refugees into that cauldron of angst? The refugees and immigrants present the opportunity to give a name and a face to the fears that plague them. As such, they become a target for aggression. For the recently liberated Easterners, the new freedom from censorship means being able to say, ‘We don’t want foreigners.’”

As deputy mayor of Frankfurt, Cohn-Bendit dealt with the multicultural challenge up close. In those days already, 25% of the population was foreign-born. This experience led him to propose “tightening” German immigration and asylum laws, for which he was, in his words, “greeted with scorn and controversy by the old left, which steadfastly supports open borders at all costs.”

Zooming out to the big picture, he said: “I would like to see a world where no individual is obliged to leave their place of birth to seek safety, opportunity or even the basic necessities of life. Alas, that is not the world we live in. We live in a global society that is highly unequal with respect to chances in life.

“Unless the next 20 years can bring hope to the children of the poor South and East, the run on our borders won’t stop. Germans must adjust to this reality and impose limits but also realize we are already an immigrant society” that democracy must accommodate. Read Noema in print.

President von Weizsäcker wrote that Germans, above all, must respect the dignity of all persons given its past. Yet he acknowledged that the asylum laws were not designed for a “massive influx of foreigners” and that the bottleneck must be broken by a new system “that controls and limits immigration as well as protects the true right of asylum.”

Even as the passions of renewed nationalism stirred at the grassroots, the leadership of Europe was moving in the opposite direction. In NPQ’s forum, foreign minister Genscher said: “The new civilization of coexistence within our European community must never again be jeopardized by national self-interest. We must not only preserve and further develop this new civilization of coexistence for ourselves but extend it to our neighbors in the East. “

“The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West.”

In this, he was fully in tune with the mindset of the other elders of European integration shaped by the horrors of World War II. At the time, French President François Mitterrand put it bluntly: “Nationalism means war.”

The disconnect that has become so manifest today was set in motion then. The good faith efforts to avoid repeating the past clashed with a lost sense of home and belonging. That nascent alienation has only grown, not diminished, over time.

And all this was compounded two decades later when Chancellor Angela Merkel opened wide the country’s gates to some 900,000 refugees from the Syrian civil war in 2015.

The Elusive Conundrum

The conundrum of how to calibrate the right balance between the human need for belonging and compassion for the peril, struggles and aspirations of the dispossessed trying to make a new life remains elusive — and global. The same issue haunts all of Europe today, the United States and even the developing world, from South Africa to the Bangladesh-India borderlands.

In this context, it is wrong to keep saying that governments which tighten strictures on immigration are “moving to the right.” What is happening is that the ongoing incapacity to find a proportionate balance between host populations and incomers has become a mainstream concern, and democratic systems are only responding as they should.

Lessons From The German Experience And Elsewhere

What lessons can be learned from the German experience and elsewhere?

First, liberals should stop treating every expression of the defense of belonging as somehow resurrecting the ghost of Hitler. “To be human means to belong,” the great pluralist philosopher Isaiah Berlin posited in a conversation we had at the outset of the Balkan wars in the 1990s. “If the streams dry up, where men and women are not products of a culture, where they don’t have kith and kin and feel closer to some people than to others, where there is no native language—that would lead to a tremendous desiccation of everything that is human.”

Second, communities, nations or unions like Europe have an obligation to their citizens to control immigration based on criteria that ensure newcomers will abide by their norms and values and contribute positively to the economic well-being of the given jurisdiction. Societies and cultures are not closed systems, but states are bound by the fiscal realities of bordered territories. The social contract of any polity with its citizens rests on this proposition.

To that end, borders must be secure, not porous. The best formulation of this comes from the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate in Texas, James Talarico. “Our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door,” he has said, so the homeowner decides who to let in.

Absent this enforced conviction, we will see the kind of mean-spirited and cruel crackdowns being practiced in the U.S. today or on the Mediterranean Sea to remedy an out-of-control situation after the fact. Better to prevent that eventuality in the first place. As the French philosopher Régis Debray put it in an apt aphorism: “Borders are a vaccine against the epidemic of walls.”

Third, we need to redefine the concept of asylum for the times we live in. In the mid-20th century, asylum was meant to provide safe refuge for those persecuted by their governments or temporarily fleeing the ravages of war. It was never meant as a path to permanent residency or to offer a haven for the mass exodus of those from states too weak to protect their own citizens or provide them with economic opportunity.

Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states. Bad faith results from good intentions if the capacity to fulfill moral claims is lacking.

The next conundrum on this front will involve climate refugees forced to leave their homeland because of the floods, droughts and famines associated with global warming for which the industrialized nations of the North are historically most responsible.

Fourth, aging societies in the North must shed the illusion that they can live without legal immigration, and that means a more multicultural mix than ever before. Avoiding cultural, security and economic clashes as this new reality takes hold entails proactive policies for assimilation and integration.

“Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states.”

The aim must be to prevent the further formation of the kind of cultural silos of immigrants concentrated in segregated neighborhoods that evolve into economic castes, as already seen for so long in places like the Parisian suburbs. In Sweden, immigrants’ lack of necessary skills and education to compete in the job market has made them among the least integrated in Europe. The gap carries on to the children, who are disproportionately engaged in what have become violent street gangs in that one-time social democratic paradise.

Integration begins with the right immigration criteria. Canada is more successful at integrating immigrants than most because some 60% are admitted through the “economic class,” which counts both assets and skills that match labor market needs. By contrast, according to Harvard University’s Paul May, two-thirds of permanent residents accepted in the U.S are admitted for family reunification, while less than 20% are based on skills.

In areas where borders are contiguous, such as the U.S. and Mexico, and there is great demand for lower-wage employment in agriculture, services and construction, a work permit system that enables easy transit across borders but does not confer permanent residency is a sensible approach. To avoid the exploitative conditions of such prior programs, labor rights conditions need to be monitored and rigorously enforced.

Ongoing integration entails institutions designed for that purpose. In California, the majority of the population today is Latino and Asian, and mostly second generation. Though challenges remain, integration has been largely successful because public higher education serves as a cultural mixer and transmission belt to the middle class. The California State University System has 470,000 students at 23 campuses in every region of the state. Its students, often the first in their families to go to college, match the immigrant profile: 48% are Latinos and 16% are Asian.

Open Societies Need Defined Borders

Open societies need defined borders to sustain a common sense of identity. One is a condition of the other. The lack of either will condemn both to the untenable situation we face today. Among the many challenges of the 21st century, balancing belonging and becoming is the one closest to home.

stories.body:
Energy and housing costs threaten biggest decline in modern times unless bold action taken, says thinktank

Soaring energy and housing costs mean Labour is on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times, a stark analysis warns.

Three weeks ahead of John Healey’s budget, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation said Britain faces a “dire” outlook unless the government takes “bold policy action”.

The JRF predicts that, after housing costs, average household incomes will be between £440 and £770 lower in real terms in 2029-30 than when Labour came to power two years ago.

Even the lower end of that range would mark the biggest decline in living standards since modern records began in 1961, the thinktank said, and come on top of a tight squeeze in the last parliament.

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has been tasked by Andy Burnham to lead the Cabinet Office cross-government taskforces, with two focusing on turning around living standards. One is looking at short-term cost of living measures to help on housing and energy, and the other at big structural interventions such as public control that might alleviate those pressures long term.

Their work will eventually form part of the 10-year plan expected later this autumn, which Burnham began discussions about with cabinet ministers at a Chequers away day this week.

Haigh has repeatedly told officials that there will have to be “trade offs” in order to prioritise alleviating the cost of living and public control.

At the budget, Burnham has promised to offer a “breathing space” to voters and Healey is expected to offer £1bn in additional support to energy consumers; but there are concerns inside government about whether that goes far enough.

Healey is minded to rebuff a call from the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether. The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.

The chancellor is understood to be considering raising this by £100, with the rise funded by taxpayers.

The foundation’s living standards analysis used the Bank of England’s two projections for energy prices – a “central” and an “adverse” scenario.

The thinktank has pointed out that since the Bank set these out in July, real-world events have tracked close to the adverse scenario, with oil prices surging back above $100 a barrel after hostilities resumed in the Middle East.

By driving up the cost of energy, the renewed conflict has also increased expectations that the Bank will raise the base interest rate to tackle resurgent inflation. Markets are now betting on four quarter point increases to 4.75% by the end of next year.

Borrowing costs for homebuyers have already jumped in response to the resulting turmoil in bond markets – with the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hitting 6% this week for the first time in three years.

after newsletter promotion

Chris Belfield, the chief economist at the JRF, said: “Without bold policy action on living standards, families are set to be poorer than they were a decade ago. This is terrible both for families who are just treading water to get by and the more than 7 million families who are already routinely going without essentials like food and basic toiletries.”

Some forecasts have suggested the typical household dual-fuel bill could leap by 16% to the equivalent of £2,000 a year in the first quarter of next year. Given the scale of the looming squeeze, the foundation has argued for a more ambitious package of measures on energy than Healey appears minded to offer.

It would like to see a baseline level of energy offered to all households at a cheaper price, with those in greater need entitled to more of these cut-price units of gas and electricity.

Other recommendations include making benefits more generous by relinking local housing allowance to average rents; and increasing universal credit, as the Conservatives did during the Covid pandemic. This could be paid for via changes such as increasing capital gains tax rates to match income tax, it argues.

The JRF analysis of changes in living standards over time differs from those of the Office for Budget Responsibility and other thinktanks such as the Resolution Foundation because of different ways of accounting for housing costs.

Despite Burnham’s promise to correct 40 years of economic missteps, Healey’s budget is expected to be relatively modest, with important decisions on tax and spending delayed until next year. These include when the UK will implement spending 3% of GDP on defence – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.

In his 28 October statement, the chancellor is expected to focus on filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer’s government in June; and laying out how the Treasury will devolve some income tax revenue to regional mayors.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “We know families are feeling the impact of higher prices, pushed up by conflicts overseas.

“The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That’s why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, capped bus fares in England at £2 in 2027, extended the 5p fuel duty cut, and frozen rail fares and prescription charges.”

stories.body:
If recent complaints are believed, London and the UK are no longer welcoming for ultra-high net worth individuals

London was once globally renowned as the “billionaires’ playground”, where the world’s super-rich could relax in the Georgian townhouses of Mayfair undisturbed by the grasping hand of the state.

But if recent complaints by fleeing ultra-high net worth individuals are to be believed, the city is no longer as welcoming for those who consider themselves to be Britain’s most-persecuted minority.

They complain of Labour’s stricter tax regime and the antipathy of others towards those with extreme wealth. One even suggested that he was leaving the country because of London’s low-traffic neighbourhoods.

“If I want to organise a gathering now, I have to take into account a lot of my friends are not here any more,” said the financier Ben Goldsmith. “How the hell are we supposed to pay for health services and everything if we are driving out the highest rate taxpayers?”

This weekend, one of the UK’s richest people, David Reuben, was revealed to have left the UK for the tax haven of Monaco. The 88-year-old is a property tycoon and Newcastle United shareholder who, along with his younger brother, Simon Reuben, has a combined estimated net worth of nearly £28bn. A spokesperson did not expand on why he left, but tax is thought to be a factor.

Sir Peter Lampl, the millionaire founder of the Sutton Trust charity, said he had moved to the US because of Sadiq Khan’s traffic policies, complaining that motorists are “pariahs” in London.

Another billionaire, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who owns the chemicals company Ineos, has said he can see why rich people are leaving the UK, describing the country as “on the slide”. Ratcliffe, who fled Britain for Monaco in 2018, complained that “the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”.

Others, meanwhile, are unimpressed by the ultra-wealthy’s complaints and the warnings of economic doom for the nation that each new announced exit tends to bring.

Arun Advani, director of CenTax, who is influential in Labour circles and helped design a hiked inheritance tax, said he was unconcerned about billionaire flight.

“Mobility among billionaires is high,” he said. “Many wealthy people leave every year, it just isn’t always reported as loudly as at the moment. So a couple of highly reported examples don’t in themselves indicate anything has changed.”

Multimillionaire Dale Vince said ultra-wealthy individuals need to “stop whingeing”. He confirmed he will be staying in the UK, and added: “The tax system is already skewed in favour of rich people. We have so many allowances, loopholes and exemptions.”

For better or worse, the data shows a clear trend; an analysis of Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index has found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024. This represents more than half of all billionaire wealth. Among those who have left are Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and shipping magnate John Fredriksen.

Rachel Reeves’ removal of the “non-dom” system, which allowed individuals to only pay tax on income generated in the UK, is blamed for many of the exits. Others say they fear new taxes on property as well as hiked inheritance taxes.

Sir James Dyson, worth £12bn, faced criticism for moving to Singapore in 2019, after telling the country to vote Brexit. He returned in 2021, and has been investing in businesses in the UK ever since.

Denise Coates, founder of gambling company bet365, is worth £8bn and appears to have no plans to leave the country. Billionaire John Caudwell, who founded phones4U, confirmed he was remaining resident in the UK.

There are even some super-rich folk coming to the UK – albeit not universally popular ones. Crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave Reform UK leader Nigel Farage a controversial £5m undeclared gift before he was elected as an MP in 2024, recently registered himself as a UK resident. So did Ben Delo, another crypto billionaire , who has given tens of millions to the party.

Paddy Renouf, who runs luxury concierge service Serendipity , says his ultra-rich clients are still in the UK and spending money.

“I am puzzled as much as anybody else about the rumours of the exodus. England is incomparable to the super-rich. There is no culture as rich with art, restaurants or history; Monaco and Dubai cannot compete on that level.”

He did concede there was some “nervousness” among his clients, adding: “Very wealthy people don’t mind paying taxes if they can anticipate them. But there is a lot of uncertainty at the moment. It is bad if we do lose them.”

Philip Munro, partner at law firm Withers, said more entrepreneurs are asking about leaving the UK, and a steady stream of reports that their peers are also leaving has “concentrated their minds”.

He blames capital gains tax and removal of business property relief on inheritance tax and said inquiries are coming in about moving residency to Dubai, Greece, Italy, Monaco and Switzerland.

Goldsmith agreed that there is “herd behaviour” caused by “social media hype” around the UK’s supposed hostility to the rich.

He added: “People overestimate crime and tax, they underestimate the downsides of living elsewhere.

“London was a hub for foreign billionaires. They pay a lot of tax, they hire a lot of people, they spend a lot of money, they are the most mobile people around, so getting money out of them is an art form.

“There’s nothing to force them to stay here; you have to attract them, and we were once good at that.”

Vince has less sympathy. Pointing at Ratcliffe’s exit as an example, he said: “He got rich here and then made off to Monaco to save himself money.

“He avoided giving back to the economy that made him a billionaire and now he bangs on that it is a bad place to do business when he became a billionaire here!

“It’s pathetic. He and anyone else who leaves here to not pay tax should be stripped of their honours.”

stories.title: What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits?
stories.summary: BBC Verify looks into the party's move to overhaul the tax that is levied on inherited wealth.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has announced she will overhaul inheritance tax if her party wins the next general election.

She told the Conservatives' annual conference that "nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home" and couples will be able to leave an additional £1m tax free.

Tax experts say the party's £6bn per year estimate of the cost of the plan is reasonable, but warn the policy would primarily benefit wealthier households and could discourage older people from moving to smaller homes.

BBC Verify has looked into the details of the policy.

How will it work?

Under the current system, inheritance tax of 40% is paid when someone's estate - the total value of their money and property - exceeds £325,000. Anything under this amount is not taxed.

And, when a person dies, they can currently transfer this tax-free allowance to a surviving spouse or civil partner which increases the combined threshold for a couple to £650,000.

On top of this individuals can get an additional transferable allowance for a family home of £175,000 each when it is left to children or other direct descendants.

So at present most married couples can potentially leave £1m without paying inheritance tax.

The Conservative plan would increase the £325,000 threshold - the point at which you start paying the tax - to £500,000 and fully exempt a family home from inheritance tax.

At the moment an estate with a £2m house could be liable for £400,000 in inheritance tax. That would reduce to zero under the Conservatives.

How many people currently pay inheritance tax?

Official figures show that in 2024-25 around 30,400 deaths in the UK left estates which were liable for inheritance tax.

This was around 5% of all UK deaths in that year.

But the number of estates paying inheritance tax is set to rise, due to the increasing value of inherited wealth being passed on and the threshold having been frozen.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated that by 2032-33 around 12% of people will have inheritance tax due either on their own death or that of their spouse or civil partner.

Citing analysis by the consultancy Oxford Economics, the Conservatives say the number of estates paying the tax will rise to 52,100 in 2029-30.

How many people would benefit from the Conservative policy?

The Conservatives estimate their reforms would reduce the number of affected estates in 2030 to 22,000.

Official data shows higher value estates pay the majority of the inheritance tax collected.

The IFS has estimated that if inheritance tax were to be entirely scrapped, which Badenoch has identified as a longer term aspiration, the wealthiest 1% of estates - those worth £2.1m or more - would get half of the benefit of the tax reduction.

And one long-standing criticism of inheritance tax is that the wealthy use legal ways to avoid paying it like putting their assets into family trusts to reduce the amount of inheritance tax ultimately due from their estates when they die.

In 2023-24, estates with a valuation of £10m only paid an average effective inheritance tax rate of 18%, according to estimates from HM Revenue and Customs.

Responding to Wednesday's conference announcement, the IFS said: "The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes – and their descendants.

"This is a very well-off group, mainly living in London and the South-East of England."

What would be the cost of this tax cut?

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the official forecaster, estimates inheritance tax will raise £9.5bn in 2026-27 - equivalent to around 0.3% of GDP.

The OBR projects this will rise to £14.5bn in 2030-31 or 0.4% of GDP.

The Conservatives estimate their plan would cost £6bn a year in 2029-30, based on Oxford Economics' analysis.

The party says it has identified £71bn in annual savings including £36bn a year from welfare cuts.

Prof Andy Summers, director of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation, told BBC Verify this was "just about about the worst possible way to deliver an inheritance tax cut".

"Exempting the family home however much it's worth will just encourage older people to concentrate their savings in their home, prevent downsizing, and so further gum up the housing market," he said.

The Conservatives argue in their press release accompanying the policy announcement that inheritance taxes are "bad for growth".

But analysis by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development suggests inheritance taxes in general are less damaging to economic growth than taxes on income from work.

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett
